name: Writing Statistical Code with AI
title: Writing Statistical Code with AI
answer: Writing statistical code with AI covers the use of AI assistants, such as large language models, to help write, edit, and debug code for statistical analysis. This includes data cleaning, model fitting, simulation, and visualization in languages like R, Python, and Julia. It also covers the reproducibility of that code, meaning that the analysis can be run again and produce the same results. The topic is not about building AI models, but about using AI as a tool in the statistical workflow.

sections.body: Writing statistical code with AI covers the use of AI assistants, such as large language models, to help write, edit, and debug code for statistical analysis. This includes data cleaning, model fitting, simulation, and visualization in languages like R, Python, and Julia. It also covers the reproducibility of that code, meaning that the analysis can be run again and produce the same results. The topic is not about building AI models, but about using AI as a tool in the statistical workflow.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: AI coding assistants typically run as extensions in code editors like VS Code, or as plugins for integrated development environments like RStudio. They may also run in notebooks such as Jupyter or Quarto. The underlying models are often accessed via cloud APIs, though some run locally. Version control systems like Git are essential for tracking changes, and package managers like renv or conda help manage dependencies. Compute can be local or on a cluster, depending on the size of the data and models.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A statistician might prompt an AI assistant to generate a function for a particular model, then review and test the output. The work involves iterative prompting, checking that the code matches the intended statistical method, and writing unit tests to verify correctness. AI can also be used to explain unfamiliar code, translate between languages, or suggest improvements. Reproducibility is maintained by documenting the prompts, the AI model version, and the final code, often in a script or notebook that can be rerun.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: AI-generated code may have unclear copyright, and some licenses restrict commercial use. There is a risk that the AI produces code with bugs or that it uses a method that is not appropriate for the data. Provenance matters, so teams need to know which parts of the code were AI-generated and which were written by a human, and this can be recorded in commit messages or metadata. Data privacy is a concern if prompts include sensitive data, and institutions and journals may have policies about disclosing AI use.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Future developments may include AI assistants that understand statistical assumptions and can warn about violations. They might integrate with reproducibility tools to automatically generate documentation and provenance records. There is also interest in AI agents that can run entire analyses, though human oversight remains important. The field is likely to see more specialized models trained on statistical code and documentation.
